**Aberystwyth Lifeboat Station** (Welsh: _Gorsaf Bad Achub Aberystwyth_) is located at South Marine Terrace, in the coastal resort of Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, which sits on Cardigan Bay, on the west coast of Wales.
A lifeboat was first placed at Aberystwyth in 1843. Management of the station was taken over by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) in 1862.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-LBES_2025-1)
In 2023, the station received a new B-class (Atlantic 85) Inshore lifeboat, RNLB _Florence and Ernest Bowles_ (B-937), which is launched by submersible tractor. The station also has a smaller Arancia-class Inshore lifeboat, _Wren_ (A-78).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeonardDenton2025130-2)

The first lifeboat at Aberystwyth was a 26-foot, 6-oared Palmer-class lifeboat, funded by the Aberystwyth Harbour Trust, and under the control of the harbour master. No records of any service carried out have been found. The boat was condemned in 1861.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-LBL1-2-3)
It is said that there were calls for a lifeboat service at Aberystwyth, after the wreck of the _Aquila_ on 19 February 1861, whilst on passage from Llanelli to Aberdovey.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Times300361-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Aquila-5)
In 1862, the RNLI took over the station, completing a chain of RNLI stations along the coast of Cardigan Bay from Strumble Head to the Llŷn Peninsula. A new 32-foot 10-oared self-righting 'pulling and sailing' (P&S) lifeboat, one with oars and sails, was placed at the station, and named _Evelyn Wood_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Aberystwyth_RNLI-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Points-7)
1875 Lifeboat House on Queen's Road

The first lifeboat house was built on Victoria terrace, near to the Glengower Hotel today. It cost £125-5s-6d. In 1875, a new boathouse was constructed on Queens Road, at a cost of £250. This was later used as a BBC studio between 1990 and 2000, and then a store for Ceredigion County Council. Since 2020, it has been used by Ceredigion Archives, with regulated temperature and humidity, following a grant from the Welsh Government.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Archives-8)
On 20 February 1877, crew member John James succumbed to cold and exhaustion, after enduring a six-hour service to rescue three men from the schooner_Sarah Ellen_ of Liverpool. The station now awards the _John James Award for Outstanding Commitment_ annually to crew members.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Sarah_Ellen-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Award-10)
A severe gale on 29 December 1900 saw Coxswain David Williams launch the lifeboat to a fishing smack; in heavy seas three lifeboatmen (Jack Williams, Tom Jones and J.C. Rea) were thrown overboard but were rescued by their fellow crewmen. Despite the loss of most of their oars, they managed to beach the lifeboat and hold it until the tide ebbed. In the meantime the fishermen, whose boat was wrecked on the rocks, made it safely to shore.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-11)
In February 1946 _Frederick Angus_ (ON 757) was at sea for more than 24 hours in severe weather standing by the broken-down submarine HMS _Universal_ and helping to rescue her crew.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-12)

In 1964, the Liverpool-class lifeboat _Aguila Wren_ (ON 892) was withdrawn, and Aberystwyth became the first RNLI lifeboat station to change from offshore to solely inshore lifeboats.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Peoples-13)
Aberystwyth's Atlantic 75-class RNLB _Enid Mary_ (B-704)
Talus MB-4H Launching Tractor
The Arancia IRB was placed at Aberystwyth in 2011 and was dedicated in Holy Trinity Church, believed to be the first and only lifeboat to be dedicated within a church.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-15)
This station is classed as an RNLI "Observe" lifeboat station; it welcomes visitors via appointment. Groups (schools, clubs, organisations) who wish to visit the station can request a tour and presentation via the stations website.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_Lifeboat_Station#cite_note-Aberystwyth_RNLI-6)

## RNLI Aberystwyth
The RNLI Lifeboat station in Aberystwyth celebrates its 150th anniversary in 2011, but the town has had a lifeboat since 1843. The lifeboat station was under the control of the Harbour Master to begin with.
The RNLI arrived in Aberystwyth in 1861, with the lifeboat 'Evelyn Wood', which cost £170. The boat was presented to the station in November 1861, and worked until 1876. During that period it was called out 13 times and saved 16 lives.
The lifeboat house at that time was situated on Victoria Terrace, near the Glengower Hotel today. The house was built for £125 5s 6d, and the builder was paid £5 extra for clearing rubble which was already on the site. It took two months to build.
texts.1:
## A new home for the lifeboat
The boat 'Evelyn Wood' carried a crew of 13 men, and was driven by ten oars, so a large number of people were needed to launch it. It was launched from the beach in the early days, and there were problems as the beach changed every day with the tides, so a slipway had to be built from the promenade to the water. The present jetty is on the site of the old slipway.
A new hut to hold a bigger lifeboat was built in 1885 on Queens Road. The RNLI used pull and row lifeboats until November 1932, when a motor boat arrived for the first time. The name of the last Aberystwyth pull and row boat was the 'John & Naomi Beattie'. In the RNLI's first 70 years in Aberystwyth, 52 lives were saved in 38 calls. When the first motor boat arrived in Aberystwyth, the Helmsman, David Williams, decided to retire after 42.5 years. He still holds the record for serving longest as Helmsman!
The new motor boat 'Frederick Angus' was 35 feet and 6 inches long, and cost £3,326 to build in 1932. It saved 25 lives during its 17 years of service in Aberystwyth. It was kept busy during World War II searching for planes forced to land in the sea. The 'Frederick Angus' was damaged in rough seas in 1949, and so was replaced by 'Lady Harrison', a boat from the Navy. It served for a period of two years.
texts.2:
## Inshore Lifeboat - (ILB)
During the summer of 1951 the 'Aguilla Wren' came to Aberystwyth, a 35 feet 6 inches Liverpool Class boat. It cost £14,142 to build. It had a double diesel engine, and could reach a speed of 8 knots. It had a medium wave radio, and this was the first motor only boat to work in Aberystwyth. The 'Aguilla Wren' served until October 1964, and saved 14 lives during that period.
In 1963 the RNLI decided to introduce Inshore Life Boats (ILBs) as an experiment, and Aberystwyth was the first station in Britain to get one. It was a hot topic at the time; many people that a dinghy with an outboard motor would be ineffective as a lifeboat. They were proved wrong, and a year later the RNLI removed the 'Aguilla Wren' from the station and ILBs have been used since then.
Between 1963 and 1983, Aberystwyth station had three Class D Inshore Life Boats, with 40 hp single motors and VHF radio. They had a crew of two or three and could reach a speed of 20 knots. They were easy and quick to launch as they did not need a large crew.
texts.3:
## The present station
The original ILBs were stored in an old warehouse at the side of the quay and would be launched down the slipway to the harbour. The warehouse was extended in 1983 in order to keep a Class C ILB which was bigger than the previous ones. This had a 40 horsepower double motor and could reach a speed of 27 knots. It carried a crew of three or four, but as it weighed nearly three quarters of a ton, it needed a tractor to launch and retrieve it. The tractor was especially designed for the RNLI and can work in water four feet deep!
Following the 1990 coastal review, the RNLI decided to upgrade Aberystwyth's facilities. A new shed was built which was big enough to keep a new Atlantic 21 ILB at the bottom of the quay. This boat could right itself if it capsized, and it arrived in Aberystwyth in June 1993. The boat represented the RNLI's commitment to Aberystwyth.
It ws replaced by the Atlantic 75 ILB 'Enid Mary' a year later. The 'Enid Mary' was launched twenty times during 1994, saving three lives! In 2011, a century and a half since the RNLI came to the town, the 'Enid Mary' is still here and going strong.
Do you have any photographs to go with this story? Please upload them to the People's Collection Wales website.

### Mechanisation and two world wars
The creation of the Irish Free State in 1922 resulted in the RNLI operating in two countries, however the new Irish government was glad to see the lifeboat service continue as it was.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-lifeboat-498-19)
The first International Lifeboat Conference was held in London in 1924 on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the RNLI. Eight other countries sent delegations and it resulted in the establishment of the International Lifeboat Federation later that year. This is now known as the International Maritime Rescue Federation and has member organisations (including the RNLI) from more than 50 countries.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009253-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-21)
Construction of motor lifeboats, first petrol-engined but later with specialised diesel engines, resumed after the war. The switch to diesel power was because these used less fuel and could cover much larger distances.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009126%E2%80%93129-22) The Second World War again brought restrictions, but by now the fleet was largely motorised. In 1918 there had been 233 'pulling and sailing' lifeboats and 23 steam or petrol. In 1939, there were just 15 unpowered lifeboats, and the greater range of the motor lifeboats meant that only 145 were needed.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009105%E2%80%93109-17)

### Mechanisation and two world wars
The RNLI's depot was moved from Poplar to Borehamwood in July 1939, a few months before the outbreak of the Second World War. The headquarters staff were also moved from London to Borehamwood during the war.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-lifeboat89-12)
The war placed considerable extra demands on the RNLI, particularly in south and east England where the threat of invasion and enemy activity was ever-present,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Leach-23) rescuing downed aircrew a frequent occurrence, and the constant danger of mines.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Foley-24) During the war, 6,376 lives were saved.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009113-25)

### Mechanisation and two world wars
Nineteen RNLI lifeboats sailed to Dunkirk between 27 May and 4 June 1940 to assist with the Dunkirk evacuation. Lifeboats from Ramsgate, (RNLB _Prudential_ (ON 697)), and Margate, (RNLB _Lord Southborough_(ON 688)), went directly to France with their own crews, Ramsgate's crew collecting 2,800 troops. Both coxswains, Edward Parker from Margate and Howard Primrose Knight from Ramsgate were awarded the Distinguished Service Medal for their "gallantry and determination when ferrying troops from the beaches".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-26) Of the other lifeboats and crews summoned to Dover by the Admiralty, the first arrivals questioned the details of the service, in particular the impracticality of running heavy lifeboats on to the beach, loading them with soldiers, then floating them off. The dispute resulted in the first three crews being sent home. Subsequent lifeboats arriving were commandeered without discussion, much to the disappointment of many lifeboatmen. A later RNLI investigation resulted in the dismissal of two Hythe crew members, who were nevertheless vindicated in one aspect of their criticism, as Hythe's _Viscountess Wakefield_ was run on to the beach at La Panne and unable to be refloated; she was the only lifeboat to be lost in the operation. Some RNLI crew members stayed in Dover for the emergency to provide repair and refuelling facilities, and after the end of the evacuation most lifeboats returned to their stations with varying levels of damage and continued their lifesaving services.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Leach-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Foley-24)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-27)

### Developments after the war
[edit]
An Arun-class lifeboat
The diesel engines used in lifeboats continued to be developed after the war. A standard Gardner engine was found to work well in the marine environment and became the RNLI's standard from 1954. Using a commercial engine made maintenance and obtaining spare parts much easier than with the specialised engines used previously.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009126%E2%80%93129-22)
Faster lifeboats were developed from the 1960s by adopting new hull shapes. The first was the Waveney-class based on an American design, but the RNLI developed the concept with the Arun-class in the 1970s. Faster craft allowed the location of stations to be reviewed with the aim of being able to reach 95% of casualties within 30 minutes of launch. This meant that some stations could be closed as there were others nearby, but it also showed some gaps in coverage which required new stations to be opened.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling200683%E2%80%9393-28)

### Developments after the war
For more than 100 years, most lifeboat launches had been to commercial vessels that were in distress. Improved engines and safety equipment, along with a reduction in coastal traffic, saw a reduction in these demands, however more leisure users were taking to the water. These people generally had less experience of the sea and were close to shore. The RNLI considered the use of small inflatable rescue boats. One was purchased for trials and the work of the lifesaving society in Brittany was studied.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling200694%E2%80%9399-29) The first of these D-class lifeboats was deployed in 1963 and by 1969, there were 108 in service which had been launched 1,210 times and saved 541 lives.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009150-30) Larger inshore lifeboats were developed with the Atlantic 21 entering service in 1970.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling200694%E2%80%9399-29)
The headquarters and depot were both moved to Poole in 1974.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-lifeboat89-12) A new Lifeboat Support Centre and College were opened on the adjacent site 2004.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-hq-31)

### New services for the new century
[edit]
RNLI lifeguards on duty at Sennen in Cornwall
The RNLI made a study of its operations during the 1990s and concluded that little more could be done to save people after accidents at sea, but there was scope to reduce the number of accidents happening. This entailed establishing some new services that do not directly involve traditional lifeboats stationed around the coast. A 'Sea Safety' campaign produces various short guides with advice and safety information for different types of user such as divers, sailors and users of personal water craft. 'Sea Check' volunteers also provide inspections and advice for leisure boat owners.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling2006197%E2%80%93199-32)
Attention was also paid to people on beaches. The RNLI started to provide lifeguards on certain beaches in May 2001. By the end of the decade, the service was provided at 100 beaches and more than 10,000 people were being given aid each year.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009246%E2%80%93247-33) 2001 also saw the first lifeboat stations established on inland waters. Enniskillen Lifeboat Station on Lough Erne was opened in May 2001 and several stations were established on the River Thames in 2002.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling2006202%E2%80%93203-34)

### New services for the new century
From 2021, the RNLI was criticised for its actions during the English Channel migrant crisis as lifeboats were called upon by HM Coastguard (as are all lifeboat launches) to rescue migrants attempting to cross the English Channel in small boats. The British government praised the RNLI's 'vital work' but in 2021 politician Nigel Farage referred to the organisation as being used as a "taxi service for illegal trafficking gangs". The public response was a 3,000% rise in daily donations and a 270% increase in people viewing the RNLI website's volunteering opportunities page after the chief executive disclosed the verbal abuse received by volunteers from members of the public.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-37) In 2024, the RNLI launched 114 times to small boats, considering this as part of their compassionate service, but which represented just over 1% of their call-outs nationally and saved the lives of 58 migrants, children among them.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-38) In September 2026, with migrants launching from further west in France, they were assisted by the RNLI south of the Isle of Wight, but the RNLI was refused landing permission in Portsmouth or Southampton, and landed the migrants at Eastney instead. They were met by a large body of protestors and police.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-40)

## Rescues, losses and medals
[edit]

## Rescues, losses and medals
### Rescues and lives saved
[edit]
_Suevic_ on the rocks, 1907
The RNLI's definition of a life saved is one where the person would have died if not for an intervention by the RNLI or other third party/emergency service.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Channel2022-41)
The RNLI was formed in 1824 and in that year 124 lives were saved. By 1829 more than 1,000 people had been saved and by the end of the century the total had risen to 41,820. Between 1900 and 1999 there were 91,952 saved, the greatest number in a single year being 1,837 in 1973.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009254%E2%80%93255-42) Fewer people have needed to be saved in recent years; in 2024 352 lives were saved and another 8,259 people aided.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-report-8-43) However, 2024 was the RNLI's busiest year in the UK, with over 9,100 launches.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-44)

## Rescues, losses and medals
### Rescues and lives saved
The biggest rescue in the RNLI's history was on 17 March 1907, when the 12,000 tonne liner SS _Suevic_ hit the Maenheere Reef near Lizard Point in Cornwall. In a strong gale and dense fog, RNLI lifeboat volunteers rescued 456 passengers, including 70 babies. Crews from The Lizard, Cadgwith, Coverack and Porthleven rowed out repeatedly for 16 hours to rescue all of the people on board. Six silver RNLI medals were later awarded, two to _Suevic_ crew members.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-45)
While the RNLI exists to 'save lives at sea', it does not salvage ships and cargoes. It will tow a boat to safety when that is appropriate but does not charge a salvage fee, however it does encourage voluntary contributions to their funds. This stance was demonstrated at Newquay in 2009, when the RNLI was criticised for not launching a lifeboat in order to aid an uncrewed fishing vessel that had run aground. A spokesperson for the RNLI declared that "We are not a salvage firm and our charity's aim is to provide immediate assistance for people in trouble at sea and lives are at risk."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-46) There have been a few isolated cases where individual lifeboat crew members have claimed salvage.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-47) There is no legal reason why crew members of the RNLI could not salvage a vessel,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-49) since they frequently tow small vessels to safety, often over long distances.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-50)

## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
[edit]
One of William Hillary's concerns in setting up the NIPLS in 1824 was that people were putting their lives in danger to rescue people from shipwrecks.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Storm-26-1) Since then, more than 600 people have died in the service of the RNLI.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-YM-51)
A memorial was unveiled outside the RNLI's Poole headquarters in 2009. It was designed by Sam Holland and bears William Hillary's motto: _with courage, nothing is impossible_. The names of all those who have lost their lives are inscribed around it.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-52) There is also an RNLI memorial at the National Memorial Arboretum at Alrewas.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-53)
RNLI gold and bronze medals
The RNLI awards gold, silver and bronze medals to its crews for bravery. The 'Thanks of the Institution Inscribed on Vellum' may also be awarded for significant contributions. In the 180 years to 2004 some 150 gold, 1,563 silver and 791 bronze medals had been presented.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Lifeboat570-13-54) Significant activities may also be recognised by a 'Framed letter of thanks' from the Chairman or a 'Letter of appreciation' from the Chief Executive or Operations Director.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Lifeboat570-13-54)

## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
The _Ralph Glister Award_ was inaugurated in 1968 for the most meritorious inshore rescue boat service each year.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-55) The _Walter Groombridge Award_ was established in 1986 in memory of Brighton Lifeboat Station's Administration Officer has been renamed the _Walter and Elizabeth Groombridge Award_ in memory of his wife who died in 1989.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-56)
The most decorated lifeboatman was Henry Blogg, coxswain of Cromer for 37 years, with three gold medals and four silver. He was also awarded the Empire Gallantry Medal in 1924, converted to a George Cross in 1941, and the British Empire Medal, and is known as "The Greatest of all Lifeboatmen".[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-57) Some other lifeboat crew who have received multiple medals include:[[Note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Lifeboat_Gallantry-59)

## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
*   William Henry Tregidgo received silver medals in 1853, 1858 and 1860 for rescues at Bude, Boscastle and Newquay.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-history-60)  
*   Robert Hook, coxswain at Lowestoft from 1853 to 1883, was awarded a silver medal in 1859, and again in 1873.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-61)  
*   Daniel Shea, coxswain at Padstow, was awarded a silver medal for two services in 1859, another in 1860 and a third in 1866.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-62)  
*   Henry Freeman, the Whitby coxswain for 22 years, was awarded silver medals in 1861 and 1880.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-63)  
*   Sydney James Harris, Coxswain Superintendent of Great Yarmouth and Gorleston, was awarded the silver medal five times, for services in 1904, 1905, 1909, 1912 and 1916.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Gt._Yarmouth_History-64)  
*   Charles Ambrose Johnson, Coxswain of Great Yarmouth and Gorleston was awarded the silver medal in 1941, along with four bronze medals won in 1922, 1938, 1940 and 1941.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Gt._Yarmouth_History-64)  

## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
*   Patrick Power, coxswain at Dunmore East, was awarded the bronze medal four times, in 1941, 1951, 1961 and 1964.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Lifeboat_Gallantry-59)  
*   Richard Evans of Moelfre was awarded a bronze medal in 1943 and two gold medals in 1959 and 1966, both for rescues in hurricanes.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-65)  
*   Daniel Kirkpatrick, coxswain of the Longhope lifeboat, was given silver medals for rescues in 1959, 1964 and 1968. This meant that he was the only person at that time with three silver medals. He would be one of 8 crew lost in the Longhope lifeboat disaster, when the lifeboat capsized in a storm on 17 March 1969.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling200676%E2%80%9378-66)  
*   Coxswain Brian Bevan of the Humber lifeboat is the only crew member to be awarded with bronze, silver and gold medals for gallantry, and have them presented at the same awards ceremony. This was for three medal services carried out over just a 7-week period between December 1978 and February 1979.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-BSG-67)  

## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
*   Coxswain Hewitt Clark of the Lerwick lifeboat was awarded the bronze medal on three occasions, 1983, 1989 and 1993, followed by a silver medal in 1995, all aboard the Arun-class lifeboat 52-10 _Soldian_ (ON 1057). This would be followed by a gold medal for the service to the _Green Lily_ in 1997.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-ClarkPHP-68)
One lifeboat has received an award: for the Daunt lightship rescue in 1936 the RNLB _Mary Stanford_ and her entire crew were decorated.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-lifeboat-498-19)
In 2022, Trearddur Bay Helmsman Lee Duncan became the first crew member of an Atlantic 85 lifeboat to be awarded the RNLI silver medal for the rescue of a surfer in extreme weather conditions. His three other crew members, Dafydd Griffiths, Leigh McCann and Michael Doran, were each awarded the RNLI bronze medal.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-TBsilver-69)
The RNLI was granted a Royal Charter of incorporation 1860 which has been revised several times since then. It is governed by a Trustee Board which receives advice and assistance from a Council and specialist committees. Day-to-day operations are managed by an Executive Team of senior managers led by a chief executive.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTERNLI202528-70)
The RNLI is split into six administrative regions:[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-report-8-43)

## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses

texts.7:
### Mechanisation and two world wars
The creation of the Irish Free State in 1922 resulted in the RNLI operating in two countries, however the new Irish government was glad to see the lifeboat service continue as it was.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-lifeboat-498-19)
The first International Lifeboat Conference was held in London in 1924 on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the RNLI. Eight other countries sent delegations and it resulted in the establishment of the International Lifeboat Federation later that year. This is now known as the International Maritime Rescue Federation and has member organisations (including the RNLI) from more than 50 countries.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009253-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-21)
Construction of motor lifeboats, first petrol-engined but later with specialised diesel engines, resumed after the war. The switch to diesel power was because these used less fuel and could cover much larger distances.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009126%E2%80%93129-22) The Second World War again brought restrictions, but by now the fleet was largely motorised. In 1918 there had been 233 'pulling and sailing' lifeboats and 23 steam or petrol. In 1939, there were just 15 unpowered lifeboats, and the greater range of the motor lifeboats meant that only 145 were needed.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009105%E2%80%93109-17)
texts.8:
### Mechanisation and two world wars
The RNLI's depot was moved from Poplar to Borehamwood in July 1939, a few months before the outbreak of the Second World War. The headquarters staff were also moved from London to Borehamwood during the war.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-lifeboat89-12)
The war placed considerable extra demands on the RNLI, particularly in south and east England where the threat of invasion and enemy activity was ever-present,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Leach-23) rescuing downed aircrew a frequent occurrence, and the constant danger of mines.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Foley-24) During the war, 6,376 lives were saved.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009113-25)
texts.9:
### Mechanisation and two world wars
Nineteen RNLI lifeboats sailed to Dunkirk between 27 May and 4 June 1940 to assist with the Dunkirk evacuation. Lifeboats from Ramsgate, (RNLB _Prudential_ (ON 697)), and Margate, (RNLB _Lord Southborough_(ON 688)), went directly to France with their own crews, Ramsgate's crew collecting 2,800 troops. Both coxswains, Edward Parker from Margate and Howard Primrose Knight from Ramsgate were awarded the Distinguished Service Medal for their "gallantry and determination when ferrying troops from the beaches".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-26) Of the other lifeboats and crews summoned to Dover by the Admiralty, the first arrivals questioned the details of the service, in particular the impracticality of running heavy lifeboats on to the beach, loading them with soldiers, then floating them off. The dispute resulted in the first three crews being sent home. Subsequent lifeboats arriving were commandeered without discussion, much to the disappointment of many lifeboatmen. A later RNLI investigation resulted in the dismissal of two Hythe crew members, who were nevertheless vindicated in one aspect of their criticism, as Hythe's _Viscountess Wakefield_ was run on to the beach at La Panne and unable to be refloated; she was the only lifeboat to be lost in the operation. Some RNLI crew members stayed in Dover for the emergency to provide repair and refuelling facilities, and after the end of the evacuation most lifeboats returned to their stations with varying levels of damage and continued their lifesaving services.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Leach-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Foley-24)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-27)
texts.10:
### Developments after the war
[edit]
An Arun-class lifeboat
The diesel engines used in lifeboats continued to be developed after the war. A standard Gardner engine was found to work well in the marine environment and became the RNLI's standard from 1954. Using a commercial engine made maintenance and obtaining spare parts much easier than with the specialised engines used previously.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009126%E2%80%93129-22)
Faster lifeboats were developed from the 1960s by adopting new hull shapes. The first was the Waveney-class based on an American design, but the RNLI developed the concept with the Arun-class in the 1970s. Faster craft allowed the location of stations to be reviewed with the aim of being able to reach 95% of casualties within 30 minutes of launch. This meant that some stations could be closed as there were others nearby, but it also showed some gaps in coverage which required new stations to be opened.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling200683%E2%80%9393-28)
texts.11:
### Developments after the war
For more than 100 years, most lifeboat launches had been to commercial vessels that were in distress. Improved engines and safety equipment, along with a reduction in coastal traffic, saw a reduction in these demands, however more leisure users were taking to the water. These people generally had less experience of the sea and were close to shore. The RNLI considered the use of small inflatable rescue boats. One was purchased for trials and the work of the lifesaving society in Brittany was studied.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling200694%E2%80%9399-29) The first of these D-class lifeboats was deployed in 1963 and by 1969, there were 108 in service which had been launched 1,210 times and saved 541 lives.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009150-30) Larger inshore lifeboats were developed with the Atlantic 21 entering service in 1970.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling200694%E2%80%9399-29)
The headquarters and depot were both moved to Poole in 1974.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-lifeboat89-12) A new Lifeboat Support Centre and College were opened on the adjacent site 2004.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-hq-31)
texts.12:
### New services for the new century
[edit]
RNLI lifeguards on duty at Sennen in Cornwall
The RNLI made a study of its operations during the 1990s and concluded that little more could be done to save people after accidents at sea, but there was scope to reduce the number of accidents happening. This entailed establishing some new services that do not directly involve traditional lifeboats stationed around the coast. A 'Sea Safety' campaign produces various short guides with advice and safety information for different types of user such as divers, sailors and users of personal water craft. 'Sea Check' volunteers also provide inspections and advice for leisure boat owners.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling2006197%E2%80%93199-32)
Attention was also paid to people on beaches. The RNLI started to provide lifeguards on certain beaches in May 2001. By the end of the decade, the service was provided at 100 beaches and more than 10,000 people were being given aid each year.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009246%E2%80%93247-33) 2001 also saw the first lifeboat stations established on inland waters. Enniskillen Lifeboat Station on Lough Erne was opened in May 2001 and several stations were established on the River Thames in 2002.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling2006202%E2%80%93203-34)
texts.13:
### New services for the new century
From 2021, the RNLI was criticised for its actions during the English Channel migrant crisis as lifeboats were called upon by HM Coastguard (as are all lifeboat launches) to rescue migrants attempting to cross the English Channel in small boats. The British government praised the RNLI's 'vital work' but in 2021 politician Nigel Farage referred to the organisation as being used as a "taxi service for illegal trafficking gangs". The public response was a 3,000% rise in daily donations and a 270% increase in people viewing the RNLI website's volunteering opportunities page after the chief executive disclosed the verbal abuse received by volunteers from members of the public.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-37) In 2024, the RNLI launched 114 times to small boats, considering this as part of their compassionate service, but which represented just over 1% of their call-outs nationally and saved the lives of 58 migrants, children among them.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-38) In September 2026, with migrants launching from further west in France, they were assisted by the RNLI south of the Isle of Wight, but the RNLI was refused landing permission in Portsmouth or Southampton, and landed the migrants at Eastney instead. They were met by a large body of protestors and police.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-40)
texts.15:
## Rescues, losses and medals
### Rescues and lives saved
[edit]
_Suevic_ on the rocks, 1907
The RNLI's definition of a life saved is one where the person would have died if not for an intervention by the RNLI or other third party/emergency service.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Channel2022-41)
The RNLI was formed in 1824 and in that year 124 lives were saved. By 1829 more than 1,000 people had been saved and by the end of the century the total had risen to 41,820. Between 1900 and 1999 there were 91,952 saved, the greatest number in a single year being 1,837 in 1973.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameron2009254%E2%80%93255-42) Fewer people have needed to be saved in recent years; in 2024 352 lives were saved and another 8,259 people aided.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-report-8-43) However, 2024 was the RNLI's busiest year in the UK, with over 9,100 launches.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-44)
texts.16:
## Rescues, losses and medals
### Rescues and lives saved
The biggest rescue in the RNLI's history was on 17 March 1907, when the 12,000 tonne liner SS _Suevic_ hit the Maenheere Reef near Lizard Point in Cornwall. In a strong gale and dense fog, RNLI lifeboat volunteers rescued 456 passengers, including 70 babies. Crews from The Lizard, Cadgwith, Coverack and Porthleven rowed out repeatedly for 16 hours to rescue all of the people on board. Six silver RNLI medals were later awarded, two to _Suevic_ crew members.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-45)
While the RNLI exists to 'save lives at sea', it does not salvage ships and cargoes. It will tow a boat to safety when that is appropriate but does not charge a salvage fee, however it does encourage voluntary contributions to their funds. This stance was demonstrated at Newquay in 2009, when the RNLI was criticised for not launching a lifeboat in order to aid an uncrewed fishing vessel that had run aground. A spokesperson for the RNLI declared that "We are not a salvage firm and our charity's aim is to provide immediate assistance for people in trouble at sea and lives are at risk."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-46) There have been a few isolated cases where individual lifeboat crew members have claimed salvage.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-47) There is no legal reason why crew members of the RNLI could not salvage a vessel,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-49) since they frequently tow small vessels to safety, often over long distances.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-50)
texts.17:
## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
[edit]
One of William Hillary's concerns in setting up the NIPLS in 1824 was that people were putting their lives in danger to rescue people from shipwrecks.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Storm-26-1) Since then, more than 600 people have died in the service of the RNLI.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-YM-51)
A memorial was unveiled outside the RNLI's Poole headquarters in 2009. It was designed by Sam Holland and bears William Hillary's motto: _with courage, nothing is impossible_. The names of all those who have lost their lives are inscribed around it.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-52) There is also an RNLI memorial at the National Memorial Arboretum at Alrewas.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-53)
RNLI gold and bronze medals
The RNLI awards gold, silver and bronze medals to its crews for bravery. The 'Thanks of the Institution Inscribed on Vellum' may also be awarded for significant contributions. In the 180 years to 2004 some 150 gold, 1,563 silver and 791 bronze medals had been presented.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Lifeboat570-13-54) Significant activities may also be recognised by a 'Framed letter of thanks' from the Chairman or a 'Letter of appreciation' from the Chief Executive or Operations Director.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Lifeboat570-13-54)
texts.18:
## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
The _Ralph Glister Award_ was inaugurated in 1968 for the most meritorious inshore rescue boat service each year.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-55) The _Walter Groombridge Award_ was established in 1986 in memory of Brighton Lifeboat Station's Administration Officer has been renamed the _Walter and Elizabeth Groombridge Award_ in memory of his wife who died in 1989.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-56)
The most decorated lifeboatman was Henry Blogg, coxswain of Cromer for 37 years, with three gold medals and four silver. He was also awarded the Empire Gallantry Medal in 1924, converted to a George Cross in 1941, and the British Empire Medal, and is known as "The Greatest of all Lifeboatmen".[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-57) Some other lifeboat crew who have received multiple medals include:[[Note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Lifeboat_Gallantry-59)
texts.19:
## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
*   William Henry Tregidgo received silver medals in 1853, 1858 and 1860 for rescues at Bude, Boscastle and Newquay.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-history-60)  
*   Robert Hook, coxswain at Lowestoft from 1853 to 1883, was awarded a silver medal in 1859, and again in 1873.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-61)  
*   Daniel Shea, coxswain at Padstow, was awarded a silver medal for two services in 1859, another in 1860 and a third in 1866.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-62)  
*   Henry Freeman, the Whitby coxswain for 22 years, was awarded silver medals in 1861 and 1880.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-63)  
*   Sydney James Harris, Coxswain Superintendent of Great Yarmouth and Gorleston, was awarded the silver medal five times, for services in 1904, 1905, 1909, 1912 and 1916.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Gt._Yarmouth_History-64)  
*   Charles Ambrose Johnson, Coxswain of Great Yarmouth and Gorleston was awarded the silver medal in 1941, along with four bronze medals won in 1922, 1938, 1940 and 1941.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Gt._Yarmouth_History-64)
texts.20:
## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
*   Patrick Power, coxswain at Dunmore East, was awarded the bronze medal four times, in 1941, 1951, 1961 and 1964.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-Lifeboat_Gallantry-59)  
*   Richard Evans of Moelfre was awarded a bronze medal in 1943 and two gold medals in 1959 and 1966, both for rescues in hurricanes.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-65)  
*   Daniel Kirkpatrick, coxswain of the Longhope lifeboat, was given silver medals for rescues in 1959, 1964 and 1968. This meant that he was the only person at that time with three silver medals. He would be one of 8 crew lost in the Longhope lifeboat disaster, when the lifeboat capsized in a storm on 17 March 1969.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiplingKipling200676%E2%80%9378-66)  
*   Coxswain Brian Bevan of the Humber lifeboat is the only crew member to be awarded with bronze, silver and gold medals for gallantry, and have them presented at the same awards ceremony. This was for three medal services carried out over just a 7-week period between December 1978 and February 1979.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-BSG-67)
texts.21:
## Rescues, losses and medals
### Lifeboat and crew losses
*   Coxswain Hewitt Clark of the Lerwick lifeboat was awarded the bronze medal on three occasions, 1983, 1989 and 1993, followed by a silver medal in 1995, all aboard the Arun-class lifeboat 52-10 _Soldian_ (ON 1057). This would be followed by a gold medal for the service to the _Green Lily_ in 1997.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-ClarkPHP-68)
One lifeboat has received an award: for the Daunt lightship rescue in 1936 the RNLB _Mary Stanford_ and her entire crew were decorated.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-lifeboat-498-19)
In 2022, Trearddur Bay Helmsman Lee Duncan became the first crew member of an Atlantic 85 lifeboat to be awarded the RNLI silver medal for the rescue of a surfer in extreme weather conditions. His three other crew members, Dafydd Griffiths, Leigh McCann and Michael Doran, were each awarded the RNLI bronze medal.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-TBsilver-69)
The RNLI was granted a Royal Charter of incorporation 1860 which has been revised several times since then. It is governed by a Trustee Board which receives advice and assistance from a Council and specialist committees. Day-to-day operations are managed by an Executive Team of senior managers led by a chief executive.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-FOOTNOTERNLI202528-70)
The RNLI is split into six administrative regions:[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Lifeboat_Institution#cite_note-report-8-43)

### @richardmarsh1368
1 year ago
Words like heroes seem painfully inadequate when referring to lifeboat crews. The RNLI is one of the organisations that we can be truly proud of. I recall once, decades ago, being in Brixham Harbour in a storm. The waves were breaking over the breakwater. A friend and I were watching this spectacular event when the maroons calling the lifeboat crew were fired. At this point, total strangers ran, RAN, to the lifeboat to head into extreme danger to save people who they had likely never met. This was way beyond my understanding of heroism. If you are reading or watching this profoundly moving video, please give some money to the RNLI. They need it.

35  years  
Hundreds  of  people  flocked  to  Dunbar Harbour  on 7  
September  to  watch  Mrs  Pauline Poland officially  
name  the  station's  new  Trent class lifeboat  Sir  Ronald  
Pechell Bt in  honour  of her  late brother.  
Ivor  McPhillips,  in  accepting  the  lifeboat  of  behalf  
of  the  station, performed  his  last official duty  as  
station honorary secretary before  his  retirement.  A  
service  of  dedication  was led by the  Reverend Alex  
Noble,  followed  by the  naming  with  the  traditional  
bottle  of  champagne.  
The  cost  of the  lifeboat  was  raised through various  
gifts  and  legacies along  with  the  Dunbar appeal  - a

## 1910-1945
The first fast motor lifeboat to arrive at the newly reopened Dover Lifeboat Station in 1930 was one of a kind.
Designed to reach casualties rapidly,_Sir William Hillary_ was powered by two 375hp petrol engines, it had a top speed of around 18 knots and was nearly twice as fast as other motor lifeboats of its time.
The Dover crew pleased to be aboard their new fast motor-powered lifeboat in 1930
In one of the most demanding rescues ever undertaken, Ballycotton lifeboat volunteers endured 49 hours at sea, 25 hours without food and only 3 hours sleep to save the lives of eight men onboard a drifting lightship.
On 7 February 1936, a strong south-eastern gale with rain and snow hit the village of Ballycotton. The storm ripped rocks from the quay and vast waves swept the harbour, spraying over the 59m lighthouse.
The next morning, an SOS was received by**Ballycotton Lifeboat Station**. _The Comet_, a lightship stationed at Daunt Rock, had broken from its moorings in the storm and was drifting without power.
Coxswain Patrick Sliney (pictured) and crew launched their lifeboat, the _Mary Stanford_. They tried to tow the lightship to safety, but steel cables snapped. The lifeboat crew travelled to Cobh to get stronger cables and grab a few hours’ rest. The lightship drifted perilously close to Daunt Rock. Sliney was forced to act quickly. It took six attempts to gather the lightship crew aboard. They travelled back to shore. They’d been away from the station for 3 days, gone without food for 25 hours and had just 3 hours’ sleep. But the only statistic Sliney and the crew were interested in was: all 8 souls saved.
Friendly Neighbourhood Lifeboatman: Will Sliney. The Spiderman illustrator talks about saving lives for real

## 1910-1945
### The Marvel illustrator on his Great Grandfather’s Daunt Rock rescue
Ballycotton crew member Will Sliney is the Great Grandson of former Coxswain Patrick Sliney, who helped rescue 8 men at Cork harbour in 1936. Listen to a snippet of Will’s podcast episode below – part of our **200 Voices** series. To hear more remarkable stories, visit **RNLI.org/200Voices** or subscribe to the RNLI, wherever you get your podcasts.
The arrival of the motor lifeboat _Royal Silver Jubilee_ at Wells-next-the-Sea in Norfolk on 11 February 1936 marked the end of the iconic sight of horses pulling lifeboats through streets and across sand to launch in all weathers.
_Royal Silver Jubilee_, which was launched by caterpillar tractors, replaced Wells’s old pulling and sailing lifeboat, the _Baltic_.
The RNLI first experimented with mechanical launching in 1920. Agricultural tractors with caterpillar tracks were adapted, making them watertight in shallow water. This 3-tonne tractor was put through its paces on sand dunes during trials at Hunstanton.

## 1910-1945
### A farewell tribute from the time.
An article called **_The Last of the Life-boat Horses_**in the December 1936 issue of _The Life-boat Journal_(now _Lifeboat_ magazine) pays tribute to this end of an era in lifeboat launching:
‘Thus passes away one of the most familiar and spectacular features of life-boat work … The change has added to the efficiency of the service, but it has taken from it something of its picturesqueness … those who saw the race for the boat-house, and the team of four, six or eight horses taking the boat into the sea, will not easily forget what a fine sight it was.’
Despite having to contend with extremely dangerous conditions, RNLI lifeboat crews saved 6,376 lives between 1939 and 1945.
Lifeboat volunteers, like this crew at Hartlepool, stepped up to save lives during the war­
RNLI lifeboat crews not only went to the aid of ships that had been wrecked, but also:
*   towed vessels with explosives and secret information  
*   navigated minefields  
*   rescued downed aircrew  
*   ferried food to remote villages  
*   brought doctors to the injured  
*   took priests to the dying.
Painting of the Mumbles lifeboat crew battling to save the crew aboard the ship _Chebogue_
Fortunately, unlike the lifeboat fleet of**1914**, the majority of lifeboats available to RNLI crews during the Second World War had been modernised to give them the strength and power to cope with the extremely punishing demands made of them.
By the end of May 1940, an advancing German army had encircled the British Expeditionary Force, leaving the port of Dunkirk in tatters and its beaches the only possible way out for a rapidly retreating army.
The destruction of the port combined with shallow surrounding waters meant that big ships couldn’t get near enough to the shore for a mass evacuation. Something different had to be done.
Britain’s Ministry of Shipping put out an urgent request for all boats ‘with a shallow draft’ – from pleasure craft to private yachts – from Hull to Southampton to report to Dover, and within 24 hours an armada of some 700 little ships had formed.

## 1910-1945
### A farewell tribute from the time.
Simultaneously, the crews of two RNLI lifeboats from Margate and Ramsgate were setting out for France on rescue missions of their own, at the request of their naval-officers-in-charge.
Watch how the lifeboats helped in Operation Dynamo
Volunteer Ramsgate Lifeboat Station Archivist John Ray

## 1910-1945
### Volunteer Ramsgate Lifeboat Station Archivist John Ray on the lifesavers who braved bombs and bullets at Dunkirk.
In May, 1940, RNLI lifeboat crews from Margate and Ramsgate launched into the Second World War. Under enemy fire, the RNLI volunteers saved 3,400 soldiers at Dunkirk. Margate Coxswain Edward Parker and Ramsgate Coxswain Howard Knight were later awarded the Distinguished Service Medal for their gallantry and determination. And all crew members received the RNLI's Thanks on Vellum.
In an excerpt taken from our 200 Voices podcast series, John Ray talks about the Dunkirk spirit showed by the volunteers of one of the RNLI crews. To hear more remarkable stories, visit **RNLI.org/200Voices** or subscribe to the RNLI, wherever you get your podcasts.

## 1946-1994
In 1947, at the age of 71, RNLI legend Henry Blogg drew 53 years of service as a lifeboat crew member to a close.Over the course of his time with the RNLI, Henry was awarded three Gold Medals and four Silver Medals for Gallantry – making him the most decorated volunteer in RNLI history. With the help of his brave crew at**Cromer**, he was responsible for saving over 873 lives.

## 1946-1994
### First of many medals
The first of Henry's medal-winning rescues took place in 1917, when his crew launched four times in 14 hours in a terrible storm. Cromer's lifeboat _Louisa Heartwell_ battled 50mph winds to rescue the 22 crew onboard the Greek vessel _Pyrin_. The crew, who had an average age of over 50 and two members over 70, had to rely on 14 oars and two sails to navigate the heavy seas. Just as they arrived back on shore, triumphant and exhausted, they were told of the Swedish ship _Fernebo_, which had been blown in two by a mine. They rowed out three times to rescue the sailors onboard.

## 1946-1994
### The man behind the legend
Although Henry became a national hero for his gallant feats, he resisted the lure of celebrity. He would always praise his crew, but never speak of his own courage. A local dignitary once remarked that Henry spoke of a dangerous rescue 'as if he had merely crossed the road for a bottle of milk'.
Henry served a remarkable 53 years on the lifeboat. Even after he retired, when the maroons sounded for the lifeboat, he would be watching from the pier. And in 1954, just a few years after retiring, he passed away.

## 1946-1994
### Henry's dog, Monte
Monte (pictured left), a Tyrolean Sheepdog, was rescued by Henry Blogg from a shipwreck in 1932. Named after the Italian ship, _Monte Nevoso_, from which he was rescued – the dog spent the rest of his life accompanying Henry to the lifeboat station, and sometimes joined the crew on the lifeboat.
If you're a dog-lover too, you can help save lives at sea with this soft toy version of Henry's beloved pet dog, Monte.
Recycled Monte dog toy available from the RNLI Shop
Inflatable lifeboats were introduced to our fleet to help crews reach areas close to shore, cliffs and caves and remain the workhorse of the RNLI today. These fast and small lifesaving craft answered the need for a quicker and more agile response to rescues in areas of water that were ill-suited to the large all-weather lifeboats.
Left: The first D class lifeboat rescue at Aberystwyth in 1963. Right: Valerie Singleton aboard the D class lifeboat _Blue Peter III,_ in North Berwick in 1967
Watch: the D class lifeboat in action
In 1969, Elizabeth Hostvedt (pictured), an 18-year-old Norwegian student at Atlantic College, Vale of Glamorgan, became the first official female crew member at the RNLI. Her request to join the crew was originally met with some resistance. A ‘special case’ was made for Elizabeth to become an official crew member, after she proved that she had the ‘physique to stand up to an arduous service’.
Things have changed rapidly since Elizabeth became a crew member. Today, the RNLI’s lifeboat crews include over 600 women, the majority of lifeboat stations have a female crew member and around a third of lifeguards are women. It’s becoming more frequent to see an all-female crew.
_Pictured left, three crew members with their D class lifeboat at Dun Laoghaire_

## 1946-1994
### Henry's dog, Monte
In 1972, the D class lifeboat was joined by a new type of inshore lifeboat. One that was bigger, faster and stronger – the B class lifeboat. The idea for a rigid inflatable boat (RIB) came from Rear Admiral Desmond Hoare, Headteacher at Atlantic College, in south Wales. The first B class lifeboat (pictured), the Atlantic 21, was named after the college in 1972.
Rear Admiral Desmond Hoare, who had the idea for a rigid inflatable lifeboat
Two more generations of B class lifeboat were later introduced: the Atlantic 75 in 1993 and the Atlantic 85 in 2005 (pictured).
Due to their size and agility,**B class lifeboats**are able to operate closer to shore than all-weather lifeboats, in shallower water, close to cliffs and among rocks.
This B class lifeboat _Rachel Hedderwick_ (pictured) at Arran Lifeboat Station was funded by a generous legacy from Miss Rachel Antoinette Hedderwick.
Did you know that many of our lifeboats are paid for by a gift, or a number of smaller gifts, that people leave in their Will? But gifts in Wills also pay for lots of other things too: crew kit, lifeguard training and the fuel that keeps our lifeboats running. So any gift – large or small – will help protect our lifesavers when they go to the aid of those in danger.
Brian Bevan MBE, former Coxswain at Humber Lifeboat Station, is the only crew member in the RNLI’s long history to be presented with Bronze, Silver and Gold Medals for Gallantry at the same awards ceremony.
Coxswain Bevan and his crew launched to three medal rescues in just 7 weeks. Years later Brian recalled: ‘Spurn Point can seem bleak at the best of times but we had the worst weather I’ve ever seen – we seemed to have weeks on end of strong easterly and north-easterly winds and snow. You don’t often have to chip thick ice off a lifeboat and you could see waves coming at you like the side of a house. I’ve not experienced anything like that since.’

## 1946-1994
### Celebrity status
Becoming one of the most decorated lifeboat crew members in history brought unexpected fame.
As well as giving interviews, Brian was asked to open the London Boat Show, was the subject of the BBC programme _This Is Your Life_(pictured)and had lunch with Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II.
‘**Penlee lifeboat, Penlee lifeboat, Falmouth Coastguard, over … Penlee lifeboat, Penlee lifeboat, Falmouth Coastguard, over … ’**
Those first seconds of radio silence, when the Coastguard lost contact with the lifeboat crew, feel like the longest stretch of time in RNLI history.Not long after, the lights of the Penlee lifeboat _Solomon Browne_ disappeared.

## 1946-1994
### Always remembered
Coxswain Trevelyan Richards was posthumously awarded the RNLI’s Gold Medal for Gallantry and the rest of the crew were awarded Bronze Medals. The names of the eight Penlee crew members who valiantly fought to save those onboard the _Union Star_ are inscribed on the**RNLI Memorial**in Poole.
Watch a short film commemorating the 40th anniversary of the Penlee lifeboat disaster
Twice as fast as the motor lifeboats it was designed to replace, the 14m Tyne class lifeboat launched in 1982. It was the first fast slipway boat and could launch from existing lifeboat slipways or lie afloat in shallow waters. The name Tyne was chosen because ex-Coxswain at**Tynemouth**, Paulin Denham Christie, was a big part of the fast slipway boat project.
The **Mersey class lifeboat** – the RNLI’s first fast carriage lifeboat – was first launched from Hastings Beach in July 1988. It is a lightweight sea-going boat designed for launching from the beach via a launch and recovery tractor and carriage. The 12m lifeboat can also be launched from a slipway or lie afloat and is capable of 17.5 knots.
Built to provide the quickest possible response service – and travel further out to sea than any of its predecessors – the 25-knot **Trent class lifeboat** joined the RNLI’s fleet in 1994. It means our volunteer crews can provide a rescue service up to 50 miles out to sea.

## 1995-2004
Over the years, we've reached millions of people with our Respect the Water and Float to Live safety messages
For almost 170 years, the RNLI had responded with unflinching bravery to incidents at sea, as they occurred. Yet the realisation was growing that the RNLI’s wealth of experience and knowledge could be of help in promoting safety at sea and preventing accidents before they happened.
In 1995, sea safety bodies and marine industries joined forces with the RNLI to ensure prevention messages reached those most in danger at sea.
Michael Vlasto, RNLI Operations Director

## 1995-2004
### Prevention is better than cure
Michael Vlasto spearheaded the sea safety work. He later became the RNLI’s Operations Director. Michael started his Sea Safety work by forging links with those involved in pleasure boating, then also connected with fishing federations, diving organisations and other watersports governing bodies.
In the late 1980s, the RNLI realised that its fleet needed upgrading in order to increase the number of lives saved at sea. Enter the 25-knot Severn class lifeboat. The Severn can take on the worst sea conditions and comes into its own on long offshore searches and rescues. It has a top speed of 25 knots, a range of 250 nautical miles and is designed to lie afloat.
After helping in the Mozambique floods of 2000, the RNLI formed its own Flood Rescue Team to respond to flood emergencies across the UK, Ireland and overseas. The charity had also helped in flood disasters in East Pakistan (1971) and in Bangladesh (1988).
RNLI Flood Rescue Team (FRT) on exercise, swift water training in an Arancia inshore rescue boat
Lough Erne in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland, is home to the RNLI’s first non-tidal inshore lifeboat station. **Enniskillen RNLI** opened on Lower Lough Erne in May 2001 and a year later a second inshore lifeboat went into service at **Carrybridge**, on Upper Lough Erne. With inland waterways being increasingly used for pleasure, the RNLI has evolved its service.
Enniskillen B class lifeboat on exercise with an RNLI rescue watercraft
RNLI lifeguards started patrolling beaches in 2001, to save more lives at sea. Today the RNLI operates a UK-wide service and thousands of people rely on our lifeguards to keep their families safe every year.
RNLI lifeguards are part of a bigger picture: we strive to save every one through lifeboats, lifeguards and water safety.
