texts.11:
## 1910-1945
The first fast motor lifeboat to arrive at the newly reopened Dover Lifeboat Station in 1930 was one of a kind.
Designed to reach casualties rapidly,_Sir William Hillary_ was powered by two 375hp petrol engines, it had a top speed of around 18 knots and was nearly twice as fast as other motor lifeboats of its time.
The Dover crew pleased to be aboard their new fast motor-powered lifeboat in 1930
In one of the most demanding rescues ever undertaken, Ballycotton lifeboat volunteers endured 49 hours at sea, 25 hours without food and only 3 hours sleep to save the lives of eight men onboard a drifting lightship.
On 7 February 1936, a strong south-eastern gale with rain and snow hit the village of Ballycotton. The storm ripped rocks from the quay and vast waves swept the harbour, spraying over the 59m lighthouse.
The next morning, an SOS was received by**Ballycotton Lifeboat Station**. _The Comet_, a lightship stationed at Daunt Rock, had broken from its moorings in the storm and was drifting without power.
Coxswain Patrick Sliney (pictured) and crew launched their lifeboat, the _Mary Stanford_. They tried to tow the lightship to safety, but steel cables snapped. The lifeboat crew travelled to Cobh to get stronger cables and grab a few hours’ rest. The lightship drifted perilously close to Daunt Rock. Sliney was forced to act quickly. It took six attempts to gather the lightship crew aboard. They travelled back to shore. They’d been away from the station for 3 days, gone without food for 25 hours and had just 3 hours’ sleep. But the only statistic Sliney and the crew were interested in was: all 8 souls saved.
Friendly Neighbourhood Lifeboatman: Will Sliney. The Spiderman illustrator talks about saving lives for real
texts.12:
## 1910-1945
### The Marvel illustrator on his Great Grandfather’s Daunt Rock rescue
Ballycotton crew member Will Sliney is the Great Grandson of former Coxswain Patrick Sliney, who helped rescue 8 men at Cork harbour in 1936. Listen to a snippet of Will’s podcast episode below – part of our **200 Voices** series. To hear more remarkable stories, visit **RNLI.org/200Voices** or subscribe to the RNLI, wherever you get your podcasts.
The arrival of the motor lifeboat _Royal Silver Jubilee_ at Wells-next-the-Sea in Norfolk on 11 February 1936 marked the end of the iconic sight of horses pulling lifeboats through streets and across sand to launch in all weathers.
_Royal Silver Jubilee_, which was launched by caterpillar tractors, replaced Wells’s old pulling and sailing lifeboat, the _Baltic_.
The RNLI first experimented with mechanical launching in 1920. Agricultural tractors with caterpillar tracks were adapted, making them watertight in shallow water. This 3-tonne tractor was put through its paces on sand dunes during trials at Hunstanton.
texts.13:
## 1910-1945
### A farewell tribute from the time.
An article called **_The Last of the Life-boat Horses_**in the December 1936 issue of _The Life-boat Journal_(now _Lifeboat_ magazine) pays tribute to this end of an era in lifeboat launching:
‘Thus passes away one of the most familiar and spectacular features of life-boat work … The change has added to the efficiency of the service, but it has taken from it something of its picturesqueness … those who saw the race for the boat-house, and the team of four, six or eight horses taking the boat into the sea, will not easily forget what a fine sight it was.’
Despite having to contend with extremely dangerous conditions, RNLI lifeboat crews saved 6,376 lives between 1939 and 1945.
Lifeboat volunteers, like this crew at Hartlepool, stepped up to save lives during the war­
RNLI lifeboat crews not only went to the aid of ships that had been wrecked, but also:
*   towed vessels with explosives and secret information  
*   navigated minefields  
*   rescued downed aircrew  
*   ferried food to remote villages  
*   brought doctors to the injured  
*   took priests to the dying.
Painting of the Mumbles lifeboat crew battling to save the crew aboard the ship _Chebogue_
Fortunately, unlike the lifeboat fleet of**1914**, the majority of lifeboats available to RNLI crews during the Second World War had been modernised to give them the strength and power to cope with the extremely punishing demands made of them.
By the end of May 1940, an advancing German army had encircled the British Expeditionary Force, leaving the port of Dunkirk in tatters and its beaches the only possible way out for a rapidly retreating army.
The destruction of the port combined with shallow surrounding waters meant that big ships couldn’t get near enough to the shore for a mass evacuation. Something different had to be done.
Britain’s Ministry of Shipping put out an urgent request for all boats ‘with a shallow draft’ – from pleasure craft to private yachts – from Hull to Southampton to report to Dover, and within 24 hours an armada of some 700 little ships had formed.
texts.14:
## 1910-1945
### A farewell tribute from the time.
Simultaneously, the crews of two RNLI lifeboats from Margate and Ramsgate were setting out for France on rescue missions of their own, at the request of their naval-officers-in-charge.
Watch how the lifeboats helped in Operation Dynamo
Volunteer Ramsgate Lifeboat Station Archivist John Ray
texts.15:
## 1910-1945
### Volunteer Ramsgate Lifeboat Station Archivist John Ray on the lifesavers who braved bombs and bullets at Dunkirk.
In May, 1940, RNLI lifeboat crews from Margate and Ramsgate launched into the Second World War. Under enemy fire, the RNLI volunteers saved 3,400 soldiers at Dunkirk. Margate Coxswain Edward Parker and Ramsgate Coxswain Howard Knight were later awarded the Distinguished Service Medal for their gallantry and determination. And all crew members received the RNLI's Thanks on Vellum.
In an excerpt taken from our 200 Voices podcast series, John Ray talks about the Dunkirk spirit showed by the volunteers of one of the RNLI crews. To hear more remarkable stories, visit **RNLI.org/200Voices** or subscribe to the RNLI, wherever you get your podcasts.
texts.16:
## 1946-1994
In 1947, at the age of 71, RNLI legend Henry Blogg drew 53 years of service as a lifeboat crew member to a close.Over the course of his time with the RNLI, Henry was awarded three Gold Medals and four Silver Medals for Gallantry – making him the most decorated volunteer in RNLI history. With the help of his brave crew at**Cromer**, he was responsible for saving over 873 lives.
texts.17:
## 1946-1994
### First of many medals
The first of Henry's medal-winning rescues took place in 1917, when his crew launched four times in 14 hours in a terrible storm. Cromer's lifeboat _Louisa Heartwell_ battled 50mph winds to rescue the 22 crew onboard the Greek vessel _Pyrin_. The crew, who had an average age of over 50 and two members over 70, had to rely on 14 oars and two sails to navigate the heavy seas. Just as they arrived back on shore, triumphant and exhausted, they were told of the Swedish ship _Fernebo_, which had been blown in two by a mine. They rowed out three times to rescue the sailors onboard.
texts.18:
## 1946-1994
### The man behind the legend
Although Henry became a national hero for his gallant feats, he resisted the lure of celebrity. He would always praise his crew, but never speak of his own courage. A local dignitary once remarked that Henry spoke of a dangerous rescue 'as if he had merely crossed the road for a bottle of milk'.
Henry served a remarkable 53 years on the lifeboat. Even after he retired, when the maroons sounded for the lifeboat, he would be watching from the pier. And in 1954, just a few years after retiring, he passed away.
texts.19:
## 1946-1994
### Henry's dog, Monte
Monte (pictured left), a Tyrolean Sheepdog, was rescued by Henry Blogg from a shipwreck in 1932. Named after the Italian ship, _Monte Nevoso_, from which he was rescued – the dog spent the rest of his life accompanying Henry to the lifeboat station, and sometimes joined the crew on the lifeboat.
If you're a dog-lover too, you can help save lives at sea with this soft toy version of Henry's beloved pet dog, Monte.
Recycled Monte dog toy available from the RNLI Shop
Inflatable lifeboats were introduced to our fleet to help crews reach areas close to shore, cliffs and caves and remain the workhorse of the RNLI today. These fast and small lifesaving craft answered the need for a quicker and more agile response to rescues in areas of water that were ill-suited to the large all-weather lifeboats.
Left: The first D class lifeboat rescue at Aberystwyth in 1963. Right: Valerie Singleton aboard the D class lifeboat _Blue Peter III,_ in North Berwick in 1967
Watch: the D class lifeboat in action
In 1969, Elizabeth Hostvedt (pictured), an 18-year-old Norwegian student at Atlantic College, Vale of Glamorgan, became the first official female crew member at the RNLI. Her request to join the crew was originally met with some resistance. A ‘special case’ was made for Elizabeth to become an official crew member, after she proved that she had the ‘physique to stand up to an arduous service’.
Things have changed rapidly since Elizabeth became a crew member. Today, the RNLI’s lifeboat crews include over 600 women, the majority of lifeboat stations have a female crew member and around a third of lifeguards are women. It’s becoming more frequent to see an all-female crew.
_Pictured left, three crew members with their D class lifeboat at Dun Laoghaire_
texts.20:
## 1946-1994
### Henry's dog, Monte
In 1972, the D class lifeboat was joined by a new type of inshore lifeboat. One that was bigger, faster and stronger – the B class lifeboat. The idea for a rigid inflatable boat (RIB) came from Rear Admiral Desmond Hoare, Headteacher at Atlantic College, in south Wales. The first B class lifeboat (pictured), the Atlantic 21, was named after the college in 1972.
Rear Admiral Desmond Hoare, who had the idea for a rigid inflatable lifeboat
Two more generations of B class lifeboat were later introduced: the Atlantic 75 in 1993 and the Atlantic 85 in 2005 (pictured).
Due to their size and agility,**B class lifeboats**are able to operate closer to shore than all-weather lifeboats, in shallower water, close to cliffs and among rocks.
This B class lifeboat _Rachel Hedderwick_ (pictured) at Arran Lifeboat Station was funded by a generous legacy from Miss Rachel Antoinette Hedderwick.
Did you know that many of our lifeboats are paid for by a gift, or a number of smaller gifts, that people leave in their Will? But gifts in Wills also pay for lots of other things too: crew kit, lifeguard training and the fuel that keeps our lifeboats running. So any gift – large or small – will help protect our lifesavers when they go to the aid of those in danger.
Brian Bevan MBE, former Coxswain at Humber Lifeboat Station, is the only crew member in the RNLI’s long history to be presented with Bronze, Silver and Gold Medals for Gallantry at the same awards ceremony.
Coxswain Bevan and his crew launched to three medal rescues in just 7 weeks. Years later Brian recalled: ‘Spurn Point can seem bleak at the best of times but we had the worst weather I’ve ever seen – we seemed to have weeks on end of strong easterly and north-easterly winds and snow. You don’t often have to chip thick ice off a lifeboat and you could see waves coming at you like the side of a house. I’ve not experienced anything like that since.’
texts.21:
## 1946-1994
### Celebrity status
Becoming one of the most decorated lifeboat crew members in history brought unexpected fame.
As well as giving interviews, Brian was asked to open the London Boat Show, was the subject of the BBC programme _This Is Your Life_(pictured)and had lunch with Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II.
‘**Penlee lifeboat, Penlee lifeboat, Falmouth Coastguard, over … Penlee lifeboat, Penlee lifeboat, Falmouth Coastguard, over … ’**
Those first seconds of radio silence, when the Coastguard lost contact with the lifeboat crew, feel like the longest stretch of time in RNLI history.Not long after, the lights of the Penlee lifeboat _Solomon Browne_ disappeared.
texts.22:
## 1946-1994
### Always remembered
Coxswain Trevelyan Richards was posthumously awarded the RNLI’s Gold Medal for Gallantry and the rest of the crew were awarded Bronze Medals. The names of the eight Penlee crew members who valiantly fought to save those onboard the _Union Star_ are inscribed on the**RNLI Memorial**in Poole.
Watch a short film commemorating the 40th anniversary of the Penlee lifeboat disaster
Twice as fast as the motor lifeboats it was designed to replace, the 14m Tyne class lifeboat launched in 1982. It was the first fast slipway boat and could launch from existing lifeboat slipways or lie afloat in shallow waters. The name Tyne was chosen because ex-Coxswain at**Tynemouth**, Paulin Denham Christie, was a big part of the fast slipway boat project.
The **Mersey class lifeboat** – the RNLI’s first fast carriage lifeboat – was first launched from Hastings Beach in July 1988. It is a lightweight sea-going boat designed for launching from the beach via a launch and recovery tractor and carriage. The 12m lifeboat can also be launched from a slipway or lie afloat and is capable of 17.5 knots.
Built to provide the quickest possible response service – and travel further out to sea than any of its predecessors – the 25-knot **Trent class lifeboat** joined the RNLI’s fleet in 1994. It means our volunteer crews can provide a rescue service up to 50 miles out to sea.
texts.23:
## 1995-2004
Over the years, we've reached millions of people with our Respect the Water and Float to Live safety messages
For almost 170 years, the RNLI had responded with unflinching bravery to incidents at sea, as they occurred. Yet the realisation was growing that the RNLI’s wealth of experience and knowledge could be of help in promoting safety at sea and preventing accidents before they happened.
In 1995, sea safety bodies and marine industries joined forces with the RNLI to ensure prevention messages reached those most in danger at sea.
Michael Vlasto, RNLI Operations Director
texts.24:
## 1995-2004
### Prevention is better than cure
Michael Vlasto spearheaded the sea safety work. He later became the RNLI’s Operations Director. Michael started his Sea Safety work by forging links with those involved in pleasure boating, then also connected with fishing federations, diving organisations and other watersports governing bodies.
In the late 1980s, the RNLI realised that its fleet needed upgrading in order to increase the number of lives saved at sea. Enter the 25-knot Severn class lifeboat. The Severn can take on the worst sea conditions and comes into its own on long offshore searches and rescues. It has a top speed of 25 knots, a range of 250 nautical miles and is designed to lie afloat.
After helping in the Mozambique floods of 2000, the RNLI formed its own Flood Rescue Team to respond to flood emergencies across the UK, Ireland and overseas. The charity had also helped in flood disasters in East Pakistan (1971) and in Bangladesh (1988).
RNLI Flood Rescue Team (FRT) on exercise, swift water training in an Arancia inshore rescue boat
Lough Erne in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland, is home to the RNLI’s first non-tidal inshore lifeboat station. **Enniskillen RNLI** opened on Lower Lough Erne in May 2001 and a year later a second inshore lifeboat went into service at **Carrybridge**, on Upper Lough Erne. With inland waterways being increasingly used for pleasure, the RNLI has evolved its service.
Enniskillen B class lifeboat on exercise with an RNLI rescue watercraft
RNLI lifeguards started patrolling beaches in 2001, to save more lives at sea. Today the RNLI operates a UK-wide service and thousands of people rely on our lifeguards to keep their families safe every year.
RNLI lifeguards are part of a bigger picture: we strive to save every one through lifeboats, lifeguards and water safety.
